chapter: Teschemacher, Pee Wee, Noon and Simeon
title: Why the Teschemacher-Pee Wee style died, and Fud Livingston
summary: Chace sees the style fading around 1935, and praises Fud Livingston, who reportedly just tried to play like Tesch and Pee Wee.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Well, that's interesting to me, and, and, it, it gives me the feeling that there were a great many clarinet players around that time. Let's, well, let's say 1930, to make a focal point. A lot of clarinet players around Chicago were playing generally in that style, and the style seems to have died about four or five years later, as suddenly as Prohibition died and so on. And I don't know why.
There was one New Yorker who did it reasonably well, Fudd Livingston.
Now, how did Fudd get, figure in there? Did he get in touch with Pee Wee, or did he find it out by himself? Did he find it out by himself?
Did he find it out by himself? Well, now Fudd, now Fudd's alive, isn't he, living around Cincinnati area or something?
He found it in the family area, I believe.

Oh, did he? Yeah. Well, somebody told me that, that Fudd had recently told him that all he was doing was try to play like the other guys, namely Tesch and Pee Wee. Now, I think he did it awfully well.
